## Guided Tutorial 5.3: Building InvoiceLines in Power Query

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will build the table the rest of Part II analyzes. Instead of adding more formula columns, you will create a new Power Query query, InvoiceLines, that starts from the invoice lines, merges in the invoice, item, and customer details, and calculates the fiscal period, the product type, and a quantity check as custom columns. You will load it as a Table, reconcile it with the source and with the lookups from Tutorial 5.2, and record it on the Documentation worksheet. Because it is a query, it rebuilds itself whenever you refresh the workbook.

**Prerequisites.** You need the analysis workbook from Tutorials 5.1 and 5.2, including the SalesInvoice, SalesInvoiceLine, Item, and SalesOrder queries.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Open the Power Query Editor and import the customers.** The customer segment and region live in the Customer Table, which the workbook does not have yet.

a. Choose **Data > Get Data > Launch Power Query Editor**.
b. In the editor, choose **Home > New Source > File > Excel Workbook**, select CharlesRiver.xlsx, and select the **T4_Customer** Table in the **Navigator**. Click **OK**.
c. Rename the new query `Customer`, and use **Home > Choose Columns** to keep CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerSegment, and Region.

**Step 2. Start the InvoiceLines query from the invoice lines.**

a. In the **Queries** pane, right-click **SalesInvoiceLine** and choose **Reference**.
b. Rename the new query `InvoiceLines`.

The new query starts from the result of SalesInvoiceLine, which stays unchanged. It holds the invoice lines as Power Query loads them, without the calculated columns you added to the worksheet in Chapter 4 and Tutorial 5.2.

**Step 3. Merge in the invoice details.**

a. With **InvoiceLines** selected, choose **Home > Merge Queries**.
b. In the upper table, click the SalesInvoiceID column. In the drop-down list below it, choose **SalesInvoice**, and click its SalesInvoiceID column.
c. Leave the **Join Kind** set to **Left Outer (all from first, matching from second)**, and read the message at the bottom of the dialog, which reports how many of the invoice lines found a match. Click **OK**.
d. A new column appears at the right, with a Table in every row. Click the expand button in its header, clear **Select All Columns**, select InvoiceDate, SalesOrderID, and CustomerID, clear **Use original column name as prefix**, and click **OK**.

@fig-05-06 shows the Merge dialog.

![The Merge Dialog in Power Query.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-06-merge-dialog.svg){#fig-05-06 fig-alt="A mock of the Power Query Merge dialog. The upper table is the InvoiceLines query with its SalesInvoiceID column selected, and the lower table is the SalesInvoice query with its SalesInvoiceID column selected, both showing their first rows. The Join Kind is Left Outer, and a message at the bottom reports that the selection matches every row from the first table. The two key columns and the join kind are outlined."}

**Step 4. Merge in the item and customer details.** Repeat the merge for the two other Tables.

a. Merge **InvoiceLines** with **Item** on ItemID, with a left outer join. Expand ItemCode, ItemGroup, and StandardCost, without the prefix.
b. Merge **InvoiceLines** with **Customer** on CustomerID, the column you added in Step 3, with a left outer join. Expand CustomerSegment and Region, without the prefix.
c. In each Merge dialog, read the match message before you click **OK**. Every row of the first table should find a match, because every key refers to exactly one row, so the merges add columns without adding or losing rows. The editor's status bar shows only a preview of the rows, so you will confirm the exact count after loading, in Step 6.

**Step 5. Add the calculated columns.** Choose **Add Column > Custom Column** for each of the columns below. Type the name in **New column name** and the formula in **Custom column formula**, and click **OK**.

| New column name | Custom column formula |
|---|---|
| `FiscalYear` | `Date.Year([InvoiceDate])` |
| `FiscalQuarter` | `Date.QuarterOfYear([InvoiceDate])` |
| `Period` | `Text.From([FiscalYear]) & "-Q" & Text.From([FiscalQuarter])` |
| `ProductType` | `Text.Middle([ItemCode], 4, 3)` |
| `WholeQuantity` | `[Quantity] = Number.RoundDown([Quantity])` |

: Custom columns for the InvoiceLines query {#tbl-05-05}

Then set each new column's data type with the icon at the left of its header: whole number for FiscalYear and FiscalQuarter, text for Period and ProductType, and true/false for WholeQuantity. @fig-05-07 shows the dialog for the ProductType column.

![The Custom Column Dialog in Power Query.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-07-custom-column.svg){#fig-05-07 fig-alt="A mock of the Power Query Custom Column dialog for the InvoiceLines query. The new column name is ProductType, and the custom column formula is Text.Middle([ItemCode], 4, 3). A list of available columns, including ItemCode, InvoiceDate, and Quantity, is shown on the right, and the dialog reports that no syntax errors have been detected. The formula is outlined."}

**Step 6. Load InvoiceLines and check the result.**

a. Choose **Home > Close & Load**. Power Query loads InvoiceLines into a new worksheet as a Table. Rename the worksheet `InvoiceLines`.
b. On the **Analysis** worksheet, type `InvoiceLines rows` in A49 and `InvoiceLines line total` in A50, and enter `=COUNTA(InvoiceLines[SalesInvoiceLineID])` in B49 and `=SUM(InvoiceLines[LineTotal])` in B50. Compare them with the invoice line count in B3 and the line total in B5.
c. In B52:E52, repeat the Furniture revenue by quarter from Tutorial 5.2, using InvoiceLines instead of SalesInvoiceLine, and compare the two rows.
d. In A53, type `Lines with a fractional quantity`, and in B53 enter `=COUNTIF(InvoiceLines[WholeQuantity],FALSE)`.

@fig-05-08 shows the loaded Table.

![The InvoiceLines Table Loaded by Power Query.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-08-invoicelines-table.svg){#fig-05-08 fig-alt="A mock of the InvoiceLines worksheet. The Table holds, for each invoice line, its ID, quantity, line total, and promotion, together with the merged InvoiceDate, ItemGroup, CustomerSegment, and Region and the calculated Period, ProductType, and WholeQuantity columns. The Queries and Connections pane at the right lists every query with the number of rows it loaded, and InvoiceLines has as many rows as SalesInvoiceLine. The InvoiceLines entry in the pane is outlined."}

**Step 7. Record the query and refresh.**

a. On the **Documentation** worksheet, add InvoiceLines to the Worksheets entry, and describe its steps in the Query steps entry: a reference to SalesInvoiceLine, left outer merges with SalesInvoice, Item, and Customer, and five custom columns.
b. Add the fractional quantities to the Open questions entry as a known limitation of the quantity data.
c. Choose **Data > Refresh All**, confirm that the row counts and totals are unchanged, update the Last refreshed date, and save the workbook.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- InvoiceLines has exactly as many rows as SalesInvoiceLine, and the same line total;
- its Furniture revenue for each quarter of 2026 agrees with the lookups from Tutorial 5.2;
- most lines are flagged as having a fractional quantity, and the Documentation worksheet records it;
- a refresh rebuilds InvoiceLines without any change to the totals.

The two methods agree, which is the evidence that the preparation is correct. From here on, the analysis uses InvoiceLines, because it is a single recorded procedure that repeats itself on every refresh, while the lookup columns on SalesInvoiceLine remain in the workbook as the check that confirmed it.
